words.definition: To sweeten or purify; to remove harshness from something.
words.friendly: To take the sting or bitterness out of something — literally sweetening it, or figuratively softening a harsh idea so it goes down easier.
words.example: The editor edulcorated the harsh review before it went to print.

words.definition: Excessively or affectedly religious or pious.
words.friendly: Describes someone whose religious devotion feels put-on for show, more performance than genuine faith.
words.example: His pietistic sighing during the sermon annoyed the rest of the pew.

words.definition: Ambiguity arising from grammatical structure — a sentence readable two ways.
words.friendly: A sentence that's grammatically fine but can be read in two completely different ways, like "I saw the man with the telescope."
words.example: "Visiting relatives can be tiring" is a classic amphiboly — are the relatives tiring, or is visiting them?

words.definition: Sharp, incisive, cutting straight to the point.
words.friendly: Cuts right through the fluff — a trenchant comment or mind gets to the heart of the matter fast, with no wasted words.
words.example: Her trenchant critique left no room for the film's plot holes to hide.

words.definition: Just beginning; in an early or rudimentary stage.
words.friendly: Still in its opening moments — a plan, feeling, or process that has only just started to take shape.
words.example: The inchoative stages of the treaty were promising, but many details remained unsettled.

words.definition: A formal speech or piece of writing praising someone highly.
words.friendly: A full-blown, formal tribute of praise — think of a glowing eulogy or a speech that sings someone's achievements from the rooftops.
words.example: The retiring professor was sent off with a panegyric from her closest students.

words.definition: Relating to real existence or factual being, as opposed to abstract theory.
words.friendly: About things as they actually exist in reality, not just as ideas or theories about them.
words.example: Philosophers debate whether numbers have any ontic status or exist only in our minds.

words.definition: To bear fruit, or to become productive.
words.friendly: To finally pay off — an effort, idea, or investment that fructifies has grown from seed into something useful.
words.example: Years of quiet research finally fructified into a working vaccine.

words.definition: Anticipating or representing something as done before it has actually happened.
words.friendly: Jumping the gun in a literary way — describing a future event as if it's already finished, to make a point land harder.
words.example: The general's proleptical toast to "victory" was delivered a full week before the battle.

words.definition: Operated by air pressure; also relating to spirit or breath.
words.friendly: Usually means "powered by compressed air" — though it can also mean relating to spirit or breath.
words.example: The pneumatic brakes hissed as the bus pulled up to the curb.

words.definition: Describing God or the divine through positive statements — the opposite of apophatic.
words.friendly: A way of talking about God by saying what God is — "God is love" — rather than only what God is not.
words.example: Cataphatic theology speaks confidently of God as loving, just, and merciful.

words.definition: Based on trust or faith; also used as a fixed reference point.
words.friendly: Something you take on trust and then use as your anchor point — a fiducial mark is the fixed spot everything else gets measured against.
words.example: Surveyors placed a fiducial marker in the bedrock before mapping the site.

words.definition: A defense of God's goodness given the existence of evil.
words.friendly: The age-old attempt to answer "If God is good, why does evil exist?"
words.example: Her thesis explored theodicy through the lens of the Book of Job.

words.definition: Mutual indwelling — a theological term for how the persons of the Trinity exist within one another.
words.friendly: A theology word for three-in-one togetherness so complete that each part fully contains and is contained by the others.
words.example: The doctrine of circumincession tries to explain how Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct yet inseparable.

words.definition: To have a consequence that benefits or reflects back on someone.
words.friendly: When credit (or blame) bounces back onto the person responsible — good deeds that redound to your reputation come back around to reward you.
words.example: The team's success will redound to the credit of its quiet, hardworking coach.

words.definition: Unable to be avoided or escaped.
words.friendly: Bound to happen no matter what you do — there's no wriggling out of an ineluctable outcome.
words.example: Old age comes for everyone; it's simply ineluctable.

words.definition: Using roundabout, wordy phrasing instead of a direct form.
words.friendly: Taking the long way round with words — saying "make a decision" instead of "decide."
words.example: His periphrastic emails could have said in one line what took him three paragraphs.

words.definition: Mental dullness or lethargy.
words.friendly: That foggy, sluggish state of mind where thinking feels like wading through syrup.
words.example: A wave of hebetude hit the class right after lunch.

words.definition: Not favorable; boding ill.
words.friendly: A bad sign — conditions or timing that seem to be working against you before you've even started.
words.example: Grey skies and a dead car battery made for an unpropitious start to the road trip.

words.definition: Meat stewed or braised in sauce — properly spelled "fricasseed."
words.friendly: A cozy old cooking term for meat that's been cut up and simmered slowly in its own sauce until tender.
words.example: Grandmother's fricasseed chicken was the highlight of every Sunday dinner.

words.definition: An artificial or inferior substitute.
words.friendly: A knockoff standing in for the real thing — technically does the job, but everyone can tell it's not the genuine article.
words.example: Wartime shoppers made do with ersatz coffee brewed from roasted chicory.

words.definition: To treat an abstract idea as if it were a concrete thing.
words.friendly: To make an idea feel real and solid — turning something fuzzy, like "the economy," into a thing you can point at.
words.example: Calling a nation's "spirit" its own being reifies something that's really just millions of individual choices.

words.definition: Escaped or avoided skillfully.
words.friendly: Slipped away cleanly — dodged something, often cleverly or narrowly, whether that's capture, a question, or an answer.
words.example: The answer eluded her for hours until it suddenly clicked in the shower.

words.definition: Expressing doubt, puzzlement, or an unresolved contradiction.
words.friendly: Stuck at a genuine dead end of thought — not confused out of laziness, but because the question itself resists a tidy answer.
words.example: Socrates often ended his dialogues on an aporetic note, with more questions than answers.

words.definition: A figure of speech naming something by an associated term, e.g., "the crown" for the monarch.
words.friendly: Using a related word to stand in for the real thing — saying "the White House announced" when you mean the administration.
words.example: "Wall Street had a rough day" is metonymy — it really means the stock market did.

words.definition: To uproot; to tear from a natural environment.
words.friendly: To pull something (or someone) out by the roots, away from the place or culture they belong to.
words.example: War deracinated an entire generation, scattering families across borders.

words.definition: Pleasant-sounding.
words.friendly: Just nice to hear — a euphonious word, name, or sentence rolls off the ear smoothly, almost musically.
words.example: "Murmuring brook" is a euphonious little phrase, soft and easy to say.

words.definition: Generally assumed or supposed to be.
words.friendly: Widely believed to be true, even if it hasn't actually been proven — the "supposed" version of something.
words.example: The putative author of the letter later turned out to be a total stranger.

words.definition: A newly coined word or phrase.
words.friendly: A brand-new word — freshly invented, not yet (or barely) in the dictionary.
words.example: "Doomscrolling" started as a neologism and quickly became everyday slang.

words.definition: Angry or bad-tempered.
words.friendly: In a foul, irritable mood — quick to snap, the way people once believed the spleen controlled your temper.
words.example: He fired off a splenetic reply to the email within seconds of reading it.

words.definition: Given to moralizing in a pompous or affected manner.
words.friendly: Loves to deliver little life lessons in a self-important way, like every sentence is a fortune cookie.
words.example: His sententious toast about "the true meaning of friendship" made everyone check their watches.

words.definition: Excessively talkative, especially about trivial things.
words.friendly: Just won't stop chatting — rambling on about small stuff long after everyone else has run out of things to say.
words.example: The garrulous cab driver told us his entire life story before we'd left the airport.

words.definition: Foolishness, silliness.
words.friendly: Plain foolishness — a comment or plan so silly it barely deserves a serious response.
words.example: The sheer fatuity of the plan became obvious the moment they tried it.

words.definition: The concluding part of a speech, often summarizing.
words.friendly: The big finish of a speech — the closing section where the speaker pulls everything together and drives the point home.
words.example: By the peroration, half the audience was on its feet.

words.definition: Needless repetition of the same idea in different words.
words.friendly: Saying the same thing twice without adding anything new, like "free gift" or "end result."
words.example: "It is what it is" is a favorite tautology of people avoiding a real explanation.

words.definition: The use of very few words; terse speech.
words.friendly: Saying a lot with very little — the art of the short, blunt reply, named after the notoriously brief Spartans of Laconia.
words.example: "Molon labe" — "come and take them" — is history's most famous piece of laconism.

words.definition: Bland, oversimplified ideas; originally, bland food or mush.
words.friendly: Thin, watered-down thinking — content so simplified and safe that it has no nutritional value for the mind.
words.example: The politician's speech was mostly pabulum: vague promises with nothing you could pin down.

words.definition: Causing sleep or drowsiness.
words.friendly: So dull — or so literally sedative — that it makes you sleepy. Think warm milk, or a three-hour budget meeting.
words.example: The lecture's soporific drone had half the room fighting to keep their eyes open.

words.definition: Excessively flattering or oily in manner.
words.friendly: So smoothly charming it feels slippery — flattery laid on so thick you can practically feel the grease.
words.example: The unctuous salesman kept complimenting my "excellent taste" before every upsell.

words.definition: Quick to find fault, overly critical of trivial things.
words.friendly: Nitpicky to a fault — the type of person who finds a problem with everything, even when it doesn't really matter.
words.example: His captious notes on the report focused entirely on comma placement.

words.definition: Sluggish, mentally or physically inactive.
words.friendly: Slow and half-asleep, like a bear in hibernation — barely moving, barely thinking.
words.example: The office fell torpid in the heavy heat of August.

roots.meaning: to be numb, to be sluggish

words.definition: A steward or official managing a medieval household.
words.friendly: The medieval version of a head of staff — the trusted official who ran a lord's household and estate day to day.
words.example: The castle's seneschal managed everything from the harvest accounts to the guest list.

words.definition: To speak or write at length on a topic.
words.friendly: To really get going on a subject — talking or writing on and on, covering it from every angle.
words.example: Ask him about vintage cars and he'll expatiate for a solid hour.

words.definition: Of no value, trifling; also invalid or ineffective.
words.friendly: Worth basically nothing — a nugatory clause in a contract is one that doesn't actually do anything.
words.example: The court ruled the old bylaw nugatory, since it had never actually been enforced.

words.definition: Wisdom, shrewd judgment.
words.friendly: Sharp, practical wisdom — the kind of good judgment that comes from experience, not just book smarts.
words.example: The old captain's sagacity kept the crew out of trouble more than once.

words.definition: The common rabble or masses, used contemptuously.
words.friendly: A snobbish, dismissive word for "the rabble" or common people, used with contempt.
words.example: The count sneered at the canaille gathering outside the palace gates.

words.definition: Insolent, humiliating treatment or language.
words.friendly: Cruel, scornful treatment meant to humiliate — the kind of insult designed to sting.
words.example: He endured years of contumely from critics before his work was finally recognized.

words.definition: With suspicion or disapproval; a sideways look.
words.friendly: The sideways glance you give something you don't quite trust — a look loaded with doubt.
words.example: The teacher looked askance at the suspiciously tidy homework.

words.definition: A stupid person; a blockhead.
words.friendly: An old-fashioned, almost affectionate insult for someone being dim or dense — a blockhead.
words.example: "You clodpate," she laughed, "you've had the map upside down the whole time."

words.definition: To put into motion or action; to motivate.
words.friendly: To be the spark that sets something moving — whether that's a machine switching on or a person finally acting on an idea.
words.example: Fear of losing the contract actuated the whole team into a weekend of overtime.

words.definition: Embezzlement of funds entrusted to one's care.
words.friendly: Quietly stealing money you were trusted to look after — embezzlement, dressed in an old-fashioned coat.
words.example: The treasurer's peculation went unnoticed for nearly a decade.

words.definition: A group considered on the fringes of respectable society.
words.friendly: The glamorous-but-shady social underworld — people living just outside the rules of "respectable" society.
words.example: The novel follows a singer navigating the demi-monde of 1920s cabarets.

words.definition: Still existing; not extinct or destroyed.
words.friendly: Still around today — used for old things (manuscripts, species, buildings) that have managed to survive.
words.example: Only three extant copies of the first printing are known to exist.

words.definition: Deceitfulness; betrayal of trust.
words.friendly: Deep, deliberate betrayal — breaking a trust that someone was right to expect you'd keep.
words.example: The general never forgave his old friend's perfidy at the negotiating table.

words.definition: A regional dialect, especially a non-standard one.
words.friendly: The distinctive, local way people talk in a particular region — full of words and rhythms an outsider might not catch.
words.example: Her grandmother still spoke the island's patois at family dinners.

words.definition: A special right belonging to a person or group.
words.friendly: A privilege that's yours and yours alone — a right that comes with your role, position, or status.
words.example: Choosing the family's holiday destination is Grandpa's prerogative, and everyone knows it.

words.definition: Boldness, audacity; also toughness or endurance.
words.friendly: Rugged, gutsy resilience — the nerve to push forward and the toughness to keep going once you do.
words.example: It took real hardihood to cross the pass in a snowstorm with no map.

words.definition: To burst into bloom; also, to develop or gradually appear.
words.friendly: To blossom out into full expression — like a flower opening, or an idea finally coming into its own.
words.example: Her quiet talent for painting effloresced once she had a studio of her own.

words.definition: A weighted string used to determine verticality; figuratively, a standard of judgment.
words.friendly: A weight on a string that hangs perfectly straight down, used to check if something's truly vertical — and, by extension, any fixed standard you measure everything else against.
words.example: He used his own grandfather's honesty as a kind of plumb line for every decision.

words.definition: Gladly, willingly (archaic).
words.friendly: An old-fashioned way of saying "gladly" or "with pleasure."
words.example: "I would fain rest here a while," the traveler sighed.

words.definition: Harsh public criticism or disgrace.
words.friendly: Public shame heaped on someone in a big, visible way — the disgrace that comes from widespread disapproval.
words.example: The scandal brought public opprobrium down on the entire firm.

words.definition: Sharply sarcastic, biting in wit or criticism.
words.friendly: Wit with real teeth — a mordant comment stings a little precisely because it's so cleverly aimed.
words.example: Her mordant film reviews were feared by directors and loved by readers.

words.definition: A formal proclamation, often political or military.
words.friendly: A big, official announcement — usually one declaring a new government, uprising, or major decree.
words.example: The general's pronunciamento announced the new government at dawn.

words.definition: A person with superficial knowledge who pretends to be an expert.
words.friendly: Someone who's skimmed the surface of a topic and then talks like they wrote the textbook on it.
words.example: The dinner party sciolist confidently corrected the actual astrophysicist at the table.

words.definition: A decline of mental faculties in old age.
words.friendly: The foggy, forgetful stretch of very old age when the sharpness of mind starts to fade.
words.example: In his dotage, he'd tell the same three stories every visit, each time as if it were new.

words.definition: The side sheltered from the wind.
words.friendly: The calm, sheltered side of something — a hill, a ship, a wall — where the wind can't quite reach you.
words.example: The hikers pitched their tent on the lee side of the ridge to escape the gusts.

words.definition: To deflect or ward off a blow, question, or argument.
words.friendly: To smoothly bat something away — a sword strike, an awkward question, or an accusation — without missing a beat.
words.example: She parried the reporter's tricky question with an easy joke.

words.definition: Foul-smelling, noxious.
words.friendly: Reeking in a way that feels almost toxic — a stench so bad it seems dangerous to breathe.
words.example: A mephitic smell drifted up from the swamp as the sun set.

words.definition: A person devoted to luxury and pleasure.
words.friendly: Someone who lives for comfort and indulgence — fine food, soft beds, easy living — named after the ancient Greek city of Sybaris, famous for its excess.
words.example: A true sybarite, he refused any hotel room without a bathtub.

roots.meaning: ancient Greek city famed for luxury

words.definition: To deliberately set aside or ignore a part of something.
words.friendly: To mentally set a piece of the puzzle aside on purpose, so you can focus cleanly on the rest.
words.example: Let's prescind from the cost for a moment and just ask if the plan actually works.

words.definition: To criticize severely; also, to strip off skin.
words.friendly: To tear into someone with harsh criticism — verbally, as if you were literally stripping the skin off.
words.example: The critics excoriated the sequel for betraying everything fans loved about the original.

words.definition: To cite as evidence or proof.
words.friendly: To bring forward a fact or example to back up your point — the thing you point to when someone asks "what's your evidence?"
words.example: The lawyer adduced three witnesses to support her client's alibi.

words.definition: Travels or wanderings, especially long or extensive ones.
words.friendly: Long, roaming journeys — the kind of extensive wandering that takes you far from home for a good long while.
words.example: His peregrinations across three continents filled a whole shelf of travel journals.

words.definition: A beggar, or one living on alms.
words.friendly: Someone who lives by asking for charity — historically, this also described monks who took vows of poverty and lived off donations.
words.example: The mendicant friars owned nothing and relied entirely on the kindness of villagers.

words.definition: Extremely generous.
words.friendly: Generous on a grand, almost showy scale — the kind of gift that makes people gasp a little.
words.example: The munificent donation funded the entire new wing of the library.

words.definition: Exhaustion from lack of nourishment; also a lack of vitality.
words.friendly: A weak, drained state from not being fed or fueled — literally from hunger, or figuratively from having nothing left to run on.
words.example: By the end of the siege, the soldiers were near inanition.

words.definition: Bitter, abusive criticism.
words.friendly: Criticism that's gone well past fair and turned into an angry, bitter tirade.
words.example: The online comments dissolved into pure vituperation within minutes.

words.definition: Hostile, harmful in effect.
words.friendly: Working against you, even if quietly — conditions or attitudes that are unfriendly to your interests.
words.example: The new policy was inimical to small businesses, even if that wasn't the intent.

words.definition: Likely to cause resentment or discontent, often through unfair comparisons.
words.friendly: Bound to make someone feel slighted — usually because it stacks people or things against each other unfairly.
words.example: Ranking the siblings by "who Mom loves best" is an invidious game nobody should play.

words.definition: A person of lower rank or status; a subordinate.
words.friendly: Someone lower down the chain of command or social ladder — a junior, working under someone with more power.
words.example: As a young subaltern, he took orders long before he ever gave them.

words.definition: To feel or express strong hatred for.
words.friendly: To loathe something so much you curse it out loud — pure, vocal detestation.
words.example: The villagers execrated the tax collector every time his cart rolled through town.

roots.meaning: sacred (to curse out of the sacred)

words.definition: A natural outer covering, like skin or a shell.
words.friendly: Nature's own protective wrapping — skin, shell, husk, or rind, whatever covers and shields something living.
words.example: A turtle's shell is a remarkably tough integument.

words.definition: Innocent, naive, showing childlike simplicity; the opposite of "disingenuous."
words.friendly: Openly trusting and a little naive, without any hidden agenda — easy to mix up with "ingenious," which means clever.
words.example: Her ingenuous question — "why would anyone lie about that?" — showed how little guile she had.

words.definition: Excessive concern with minor details or rules.
words.friendly: Getting lost in the tiny rules while missing the bigger picture — obsessing over the fine print nobody else cares about.
words.example: His pedantry over Oxford commas derailed the whole meeting.

words.definition: A thorough, careful examination.
words.friendly: A deep, no-stone-unturned look at something — going over every detail with real care.
words.example: Only after a careful perscrutation of the ledgers did the discrepancy turn up.

words.definition: To raise objections; to show reluctance.
words.friendly: To politely push back or hesitate rather than go along right away — a soft "I'd rather not."
words.example: When asked to sign without reading it, she demurred.

words.definition: Superficially plausible but actually wrong.
words.friendly: Sounds convincing at first glance but falls apart the moment you actually check it.
words.example: "Everyone's doing it" is a specious argument that never quite holds up under scrutiny.

words.definition: Insincere, hypocritical talk, often moralizing.
words.friendly: Preachy talk that sounds virtuous but isn't backed by any real feeling — moral posturing on autopilot.
words.example: He was tired of the corporate cant about "family" from a company that never gave anyone time off.

roots.meaning: whining speech of beggars, then hypocrisy

words.definition: Lacking courage, cowardly.
words.friendly: Timid to the point of spinelessness — too scared to stand up even when it clearly matters.
words.example: The board's pusillanimous silence let the scandal spiral out of control.

words.definition: Fox-like; cunning, crafty.
words.friendly: Sly and clever the way a fox is — quick-witted, a little sneaky, always a step ahead.
words.example: He gave a vulpine grin the moment he spotted the loophole.

words.definition: One after another, in sequence.
words.friendly: Taken up strictly one at a time, in order — no skipping ahead, no doing two at once.
words.example: The judge addressed each of the twelve claims seriatim.

words.definition: Extreme frugality; stinginess.
words.friendly: Being tight with money (or words, or resources) well past the point of reasonable thrift.
words.example: His parsimony was legendary — he reused tea bags three times over.

words.definition: A correction, especially in a text.
words.friendly: A fix made to a piece of writing — a scholarly tweak that corrects an error in an old or important text.
words.example: The new edition includes dozens of emendations to the original manuscript.

words.definition: Moderate in eating and drinking.
words.friendly: Deliberately restrained around food and drink — never overindulging, always leaving a little on the plate.
words.example: His abstemious habits kept him sharp long after his peers had slowed down.

words.definition: A grammatical mistake or breach of etiquette.
words.friendly: A slip-up in grammar or manners — the kind of small error that makes a stickler wince.
words.example: "Between you and I" is a common solecism that still makes grammarians flinch.

words.definition: Relating to conflict within a group; mutually destructive.
words.friendly: Infighting that tears a group apart from the inside — a fight where everyone loses, because it's family against family.
words.example: The party's internecine squabbling did more damage than any outside opponent could.

words.definition: Indifferent, careless; also a person of that disposition.
words.friendly: A shrug turned into a whole personality — caring so little about things that used to matter that nothing seems worth the effort anymore.
words.example: His pococurante attitude toward the awards ceremony surprised everyone who knew how hard he'd worked.

words.definition: A confused, complicated situation or dispute.
words.friendly: A tangled, messy situation that's hard to make sense of — part misunderstanding, part drama, all confusion.
words.example: The whole seating-chart imbroglio started with one misplaced name card.

words.definition: Threatening, menacing.
words.friendly: Carrying an unmistakable air of threat — a minatory look or letter makes it very clear something bad might follow.
words.example: The minatory tone of the letter made the tenant nervous before she'd even opened the envelope.

words.definition: Strong public criticism or verbal abuse.
words.friendly: Loud, public condemnation — the kind of blistering criticism that plays out in front of everyone.
words.example: The whistleblower faced years of public obloquy before history proved her right.

words.definition: A sudden violent outburst, of emotion or action.
words.friendly: A sudden, intense burst that overwhelms you all at once — a fit of laughter, rage, or coughing that hits like a wave.
words.example: She was seized by a paroxysm of laughter she couldn't explain to anyone else in the room.

words.definition: Added from an external source, not inherent.
words.friendly: Bolted on from outside rather than built in from the start — an extra, not a core part.
words.example: The commentary feels adscititious, as if it were tacked onto an already finished text.

words.definition: Lack of knowledge, ignorance.
words.friendly: Simple not-knowing — a gap in knowledge, without any judgment attached to it.
words.example: He admitted his nescience of French wine and let the sommelier choose.

words.definition: Excessive interest in sexual matters.
words.friendly: An overeager, leering kind of curiosity about anything racy — interest that's gone past healthy into nosy.
words.example: The tabloid's prurience over the couple's private life bordered on obsessive.

words.definition: Sooty, dark, murky.
words.friendly: Dark and smoky-looking, like everything's coated in a thin layer of soot.
words.example: A fuliginous haze hung over the factory town at dusk.

words.definition: To deny or contradict.
words.friendly: To flatly speak against something someone else said — to say "that's not so."
words.example: No one dared gainsay the old captain's account of the storm.

words.definition: Laziness, sloth (from Latin).
words.friendly: An old Latin word for pure laziness — the drag of not wanting to do anything at all.
words.example: The monks preached against ignavia as one of the soul's quiet dangers.

words.definition: A shield displaying a coat of arms.
words.friendly: The shield-shaped emblem showing a family's coat of arms — its heraldic "nameplate."
words.example: The family's escutcheon still hangs above the old manor's front door.

words.definition: Outdated, obsolete, or retired due to age.
words.friendly: Past its useful prime and put out to pasture — too old-fashioned or worn out to keep doing the job.
words.example: The superannuated printer finally got replaced after fifteen years of jamming.

words.definition: Substitutes, especially in medicine.
words.friendly: Stand-in remedies used when the real treatment isn't available — medical understudies, essentially.
words.example: Wartime doctors often relied on succedanea when proper medicines ran out.

words.definition: Boastful, blustering talk.
words.friendly: Big, blustery bragging — loud talk about your own greatness that's mostly hot air.
words.example: His rodomontade about "single-handedly" saving the project fooled no one who'd actually been there.

words.definition: To use trickery or deceit to achieve something.
words.friendly: To wriggle your way to a goal through sneaky tricks rather than fair play.
words.example: He chicaned his way into the deal with a contract full of fine print.

words.definition: The pure or abstract science of learning or knowledge, often mathematics.
words.friendly: Learning in its purest, most abstract form — the deep structure of knowledge itself, especially the mathematical kind.
words.example: The philosopher dreamed of a universal mathesis that could unify every field of knowledge.

words.definition: Excessively concerned with formal rules or trivial detail.
words.friendly: Overly strict about the small stuff — correcting minor technicalities that don't really change anything.
words.example: It felt a little pedantic to argue about "who" versus "whom" in a text message.

words.definition: A flashing, sparkling light.
words.friendly: A quick, glittering flash of light — think sunlight bouncing off water, or a diamond catching the light.
words.example: The coruscation of the chandelier scattered light across every corner of the ballroom.

words.definition: A beginner, novice.
words.friendly: Someone brand new to a skill or field — still learning the ropes, not yet an expert.
words.example: Even a tyro chess player can spot that blunder.

words.definition: Extremely bad, detestable.
words.friendly: Bad in a way that deserves real disgust — not just "mediocre," but truly detestable.
words.example: The reviewer called the sequel execrable, and the box office numbers agreed.

words.definition: Blood-red in color.
words.friendly: A deep, vivid red — the color of fresh blood, famously used by Shakespeare's Macbeth.
words.example: The sunset washed the whole sky with an incarnadine glow.

words.definition: A small gap or space between things.
words.friendly: The tiny in-between space that's easy to overlook — the crack between the floorboards, the gap in a schedule.
words.example: Weeds pushed up through every interstice in the old brick path.

words.definition: Critical or censorious remarks.
words.friendly: Pointed, disapproving comments — the kind of critique that carries a bit of a scolding tone.
words.example: The professor's animadversions on the essay filled the margins in red ink.

words.definition: Impossible to refute, undeniable.
words.friendly: So solidly proven there's no arguing with it — the case is simply closed.
words.example: The DNA evidence was irrefragable, and the trial ended within the hour.

words.definition: Complexity, intricacy; also a curling inward.
words.friendly: A tangled, folded-in-on-itself kind of complexity — things wrapped so tightly together they're hard to pull apart.
words.example: The plot's involution left half the audience trying to untangle it after the credits.

words.definition: Force or effort, as in "by dint of."
words.friendly: Sheer effort or force — mostly survives today in the phrase "by dint of."
words.example: He passed the exam by dint of sheer, stubborn practice.

words.definition: Joined using a mortise-and-tenon joint; fitted securely together.
words.friendly: Locked together the old-fashioned carpenter's way — one piece slotting snugly into a hole cut just for it.
words.example: The old barn's beams were mortised together without a single nail.

words.definition: Highly relevant, apt.
words.friendly: Exactly the right fit for the moment — a comment, quote, or example that lands perfectly on point.
words.example: Her apposite remark summed up the whole debate in one sentence.

words.definition: Softly glowing or flickering (light); also, light wit.
words.friendly: Glowing gently rather than blazing — a soft, flickering light, or a wit that's playful rather than sharp.
words.example: Candlelight cast a lambent glow across the old dining room.

words.definition: A religious recluse living in solitude.
words.friendly: Someone who withdraws from the world entirely to live alone in prayer and reflection.
words.example: The anchorite lived in a small cell attached to the church for over thirty years.

words.definition: To satisfy thirst; to quench.
words.friendly: To fully satisfy a craving — most often thirst, but figuratively any deep want or need.
words.example: One cold glass of water slaked his thirst after the long hike.

words.definition: Needle-shaped.
words.friendly: Long, thin, and pointed like a needle — the shape of a pine needle or a sharp little crystal.
words.example: Pine trees are easy to identify by their acicular leaves.

words.definition: Exhausted of vitality, weak, overrefined.
words.friendly: Worn out and soft — having lost its original strength or vigor through too much comfort or refinement.
words.example: Critics called the once-daring magazine effete, a shadow of its bold early years.

words.definition: An accessory or minor attached item or right.
words.friendly: A small extra that comes attached to something bigger — the accessories and add-ons that belong with the main thing.
words.example: The lease included the garage and all its appurtenances.

words.definition: To gloss over or minimize a fault.
words.friendly: To smooth over a mistake with soft words, making it sound smaller than it really is.
words.example: He tried to gloze over the missed deadline with vague talk of "unforeseen challenges."

roots.meaning: to comment — then to smooth over

words.definition: In an early stage, just beginning.
words.friendly: Just starting to show itself — the very first, barely-visible stage of something bigger to come.
words.example: Doctors caught the incipient signs of the illness before it could spread.

roots.meaning: to take (to take up, to begin)

words.definition: Creative inspiration, especially divine.
words.friendly: A sudden rush of inspiration that feels bigger than you — as if the idea were breathed into you from somewhere else.
words.example: The poet described the whole piece arriving in one burst of afflatus at 3 a.m.
